name: Sam Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cable, lighting and switchgear for Brightline Electrical Wholesale, which supplies about 400 electricians. I drove a delivery van for Brightline for fifteen years, then moved to the buying desk four years ago, so I'm still the junior buyer. Most mornings I'm checking prices against what the electricians actually pay at the counter, and arguing with the copper suppliers. I like that I know the trade from the van. What bugs me is the end of the month, when every supplier wants their invoice paid yesterday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means steady work and no panic. I'd tell the lads at the counter that tools come and go, but a good electrician still needs a good supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel fine. I use an AI assistant every day for price comparisons, and my boss Bernard says I'm a quick learner for a van driver. We've about five months saved, and our son Kenji's an electrician, so I've got a view of both sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and use the tools more cleverly. I'd try the AI for forecasting copper cable orders, since that's where we get caught out. I'd save 200 pounds a month and not change much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I like a quiet year where nothing needs to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the electricians say about the AI tools when they're at the counter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They like anything that makes their quotes faster. A few of the older ones don't trust it, but they like it when I ring them with a price in two minutes instead of twenty. I use the tool behind the scenes and tell them it was my own work, which is half true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the fifteen years on the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the customer is on a ladder in the rain, and when he phones he needs an answer straight away. A buyer who forgets that makes a bad buyer, and I try to stay close to it.

I'd tell the counter lads that a good electrician still needs a good **supplier**.
think: I'm fine: I use AI **every day** for price comparisons and Bernard says I learn quickly.

do: Try AI to **forecast** copper cable orders, where we usually get caught out.
Save **200 pounds** a month and change little else.
feel: **Calm**; I like a quiet year where nothing needs rescuing.

steps.text: Test AI forecasting on copper cable orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should help people keep up. I'd tell the lads that Brightline should train its own people first, since a firm that grows its own staff is a firm worth working for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit uneasy. Software could do a lot of what the buying team does, and it'd be easy for a junior buyer to be the one left out in a re-org. But I'm ahead of the others on the tools, and I'd hope that counts for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become the person at Brightline who knows both the trade counter and the AI tools. I'd ask Bernard to put me on the project for AI-assisted quoting, and I'd offer to train two apprentices. If I can show value, it's harder to cut me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but busy. Busy's better than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want the firm to put its effort, if people had to change roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put it into the trade counter and the account side, where a person knows each electrician's name and habits. The back office is where the software will bite. I'd rather be the front when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the older buyers who don't use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll sit with them for an hour and show them. I don't believe in leaving people behind, and I don't believe in getting handouts for it either. Learn the thing and keep your job.

I'd say a firm that grows its own staff is worth **working for**.

I'm ahead of the others on tools, and I **hope** that counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the thing we've been warned about, and we've got two years. I'd tell the lads that families and trades will carry us through, as they always have, but we'd better start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my buying desk goes in two years, and at 60 I'd struggle to find another one. We'd have about five months saved, and Yuki's part-time wage doesn't go far. That's the honest picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my son Kenji and offer a partnership: he's the qualified electrician, and I'd do the estimating, the buying and the paperwork. I'd use AI for all of it. We'd buy a second van and put in my savings. I'd also keep the Brightline job as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but pointed. It's a worry that makes me do things, not freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think about your son Kenji's future, with robots coming around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kenji's work is hands-on, so robots arrive about 2031. That's three years after the thinking AI, and I'd say he's got a decent run. But I'd tell him to keep his own savings, and to learn the estimating side too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help, if it were offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only as a loan, or if I'd paid in. I'd rather earn it, with the van. But if the choice was my wife going without, I'd take it and not feel small about it.

I'd tell the lads that **families and trades** will carry us through.

fieldNote: Turns fear into a **family business** plan.

Expects his son's **hands-on** trade to last longer, and plans the new firm around that.

steps.text: Offer my son Kenji a contracting partnership

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if people use it. I'd say let's spend it on training, not on arguing, and the young ones should get a trade in their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a lot easier. I'd be 63, and I'd have time to grow a small business with Kenji and get out of Brightline on my own terms. It's still a risk, but a manageable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start doing estimating for a few of Kenji's builder friends in the evenings. By year three I'd want enough work to reduce my hours at Brightline. I'd keep using AI daily, and save 250 pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. It's the first picture where I can see a way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the five years would you spend on what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year goes on proving the idea with two or three customers. The second and third go on building the name. I'd leave Brightline when the small firm pays about 1,200 pounds a month, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the trade with your hands and the paperwork with the tool. If you can do both, you won't be anyone's problem. That's what I wish I'd known at 25.

I'd say spend it on **training**, not arguing, and get young people a trade.
think: I'd be a lot **easier**, at 63, with time to grow a small firm with Kenji.
It's still a risk, but a **manageable** one.

feel: **Uneasy but optimistic**; the first picture where I see a way through.
S3.quote: Learn the trade with your hands and the paperwork with the tool.
fieldNote: Sets a **number** for leaving: 1,200 pounds a month from the small firm.

steps.text: Do evening estimating for Kenji's builder friends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to plan, and the people who prepare will do fine. I'd say it's time to get our children into skills and savings, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly a retirement matter. I'd be 68, retired, and maybe helping with the small firm for fun. My worry is Aiko's pupils, who will grow up in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at Brightline until 65, use AI daily, and build the little firm slowly with Kenji so he can take it on. I'd save to six months, and then retire and help with the grandchildren.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd probably be bored, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how does your plan with Kenji change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm would be Kenji's, with me as a part-time adviser. I'd enjoy teaching him the buying side, which was never part of his trade. It'd feel like a good handover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Aiko, who teaches?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching will change. Children will always need a person to learn from. I'd tell my daughter Aiko to be the teacher who knows each child's name. I'd also tell her to keep some savings, as I do.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** to plan, and the prepared will do fine.
I'd say get children into **skills and savings**, not slogans.
think: For me it's mostly a **retirement matter**; I'd be 68.
My worry is my daughter Aiko's **pupils**, who will grow up in it.
do: Work at Brightline until **65** and build the little firm slowly with Kenji.
Save to **six months**, then retire and help with the grandchildren.
S4.quote: Children will always need a person to learn from.
fieldNote: Sees the longer timeline as a chance to **hand over** a business to his son.
Worries about the **next generation**, not himself.

steps.text: Keep working at Brightline until I'm 65

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I'd be 60 with a desk that might vanish and only five months saved. What would help is time to set up with Kenji, a chance to learn without being talked down to, and work that pays for itself rather than a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptive isn't the same as being unafraid. I use the tools every day, and I still lie awake thinking about the day a tool does my job better than I do.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive isn't the same as being unafraid.
portrait: Sam is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of electrical supplies, after fifteen years driving a delivery van for the firm.
He uses AI **every day**, mostly quietly, and learns fast, which helps him feel ahead.
Traditional in outlook, he favours **work and apprenticeships** over handouts and trusts family.
He has about **five months** saved, a wife Yuki who works part-time, and a son Kenji who is an electrician.
His main plan is a **small firm with Kenji**: estimating and buying with AI, while his son does the hands-on work.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with only five months saved and a desk that might vanish.
whatWouldHelp: Time to set up with Kenji, **fair training** and work that pays for itself.
